paras: The Bradford police shooting of Wills Abbott was a gun fight in early August 1910 at Bradford, Ohio, in which police officers mortally wounded Abbott, one of a group of Black men whose camp the officers had gone to investigate. Abbott's companions surrendered and were jailed. White newspapers from Illinois to Montana carried the story as a 'pitched battle' between police and 'a band of negroes', drawing on the officers' account; no Black-press coverage was found.

According to the fullest report, printed in an Ohio state-news column under a Piqua heading, Chief of Police George Ebbits had gone to investigate a camp of Black men at Bradford. The men, that account said, ordered him away while displaying revolvers. The reports do not say why the men were camped there or what drew the chief's attention.

Ebbits returned with Lieutenant Reed and Marshal Stolz, and according to the officers the men opened fire on them as they approached the 'rendezvous'. In a running fight that extended over about a mile, a Piqua dispatch said, 'a score of shots' were exchanged between the men and the pursuing officers. Both sides fired from behind telegraph poles and trees.

Abbott was shot through the abdomen and was reported mortally wounded, at which point the others surrendered. His first name was printed as 'Wills' in the wire report and as 'Willis' in the Ohio item.
Abbott's companions were placed in jail, but the coverage gives neither their number nor any charges against them. No report of Abbott's death, an inquest, or any inquiry into the shooting was found.

The story moved as a short wire item datelined Piqua, Aug. 3, and the East St. Louis Daily Journal ran it the same day under the headline 'NEGROES BATTLE POLICE', calling the men a 'gang' and Abbott a 'fugitive'. The Journal printed it directly above a Savannah dispatch reporting that a sheriff's posse near Pelham, Georgia, had killed two Black men. In Mississippi, the Brookhaven Semi-Weekly Leader ran the same text under 'BATTLE WITH NEGROES. Ohio Officers Pursued Them One Mile and Shot Only One.'

Most papers that carried the story did so in weekly news digests, where it shrank to a single sentence reporting that 'one of the negroes was fatally shot'. Versions ran in the Ladysmith News-Budget in Wisconsin on Aug. 5 and in the Cotter Courier in Arkansas on Aug. 12. The North Platte Semi-Weekly Tribune in Nebraska printed it the same day, and the Ekalaka Eagle in Montana carried it as late as Aug. 19. None of these digest items named Abbott or the officers.

The only account with names and detail appeared in the Greenville Journal of Greenville, Ohio, on Aug. 11, in a state-news column that gave the officers' version without comment. All the reports described the shooting from the officers' side, and none recorded what Abbott or his companions said. No coverage of the episode was found in the Black press.

reader.title: Bradford police shooting of Wills Abbott
bases: Police officers, named as a chief, a lieutenant and a marshal, shot and mortally wounded a Black man during a running gun fight with a group of Black men at their camp, with no crowd involved (A1, A4).

Two differently worded Piqua reports, a wire dispatch (A1) and a fuller Ohio state-news item (A4), agree on the gun fight, the mortal wounding of Abbott and the surrender, though both give only the officers' version.

accounts.label: Wire report (Piqua)
accounts.gist: Officers approaching the negroes' rendezvous at Bradford were fired upon; in a running fight over a mile a score of shots were exchanged, and the men surrendered when Abbott fell mortally wounded.

accounts.label: Officers' account (Ohio state news, Piqua)
accounts.gist: Chief Ebbits was ordered away from the camp by men displaying revolvers; he returned with Lt. Reed and Marshal Stolz, the men opened fire, the officers responded, and after Abbott was shot through the abdomen the rest surrendered and were jailed.

framing.detail: The East St. Louis Daily Journal headlined 'NEGROES BATTLE POLICE' and called the men a 'gang' and Abbott a 'fugitive', printing the item above a Georgia posse killing.
The Brookhaven, Miss., Semi-Weekly Leader ran 'BATTLE WITH NEGROES. Ohio Officers Pursued Them One Mile and Shot Only One.'
The Greenville Journal's state-news column gave the fullest account in flat terms, attributing the first shots to the men and naming the officers.
Weekly news digests in Wisconsin, Arkansas, Nebraska and Montana reduced it to one or two sentences about a 'pitched battle' in which 'one of the negroes was fatally shot'.

conflicts.note: Neither source is clearly better; A1 is the earliest wire report, A4 the fuller Ohio item.
